steps.body: Welcome to grade-4 territory. You know multiplication as equal groups — now it grows a second job: **comparing**. 'Maya has 3 TIMES as many stickers as Leo' means Maya's pile is Leo's pile, copied 3 times. If Leo has 5, Maya has 3 × 5 = 15.

widget.prompt: Leo's bar is 4 long. Slide Maya's bar to make it exactly 3 TIMES as long as Leo's.
widget.lowFeedback: Longer — 'times as many' copies Leo's WHOLE bar again. Count copies: one 4, two 4s…
widget.highFeedback: Too long — that's more than three copies of 4. Three copies of Leo's bar stop at 12.
widget.successFeedback: 12 = three copies of Leo's 4, laid end to end. 'Times as many' means whole copies of the other pile.

predict.prompt: Maya's bar must be 3 TIMES as long as Leo's 4. Is that the same as 3 MORE than Leo's?

options.label: No — times makes it longer than adding

predict.reveal: Three MORE would reach just 7 — but three TIMES copies Leo's whole bar again and again. Multiplying grows far faster than adding.

cml.actionGoal: Manipulate the model and track how it represents times as many.
invariants: The manipulated model and the mathematical relationship for times as many must stay consistent.
misconceptions: Changing a visible feature without preserving the relationship that defines times as many.
cml.counterfactualPrompt: What change would make the model stop representing the same mathematical relationship?

explanationVariants: 4 times as many as 6 means four copies of the 6-pile: 4 × 6 = 24 marbles.
Bar picture: Jin's bar is four 6-bars laid end to end — 24.

widget.prompt: Kim has 6 marbles. Jin has 4 TIMES as many. How many marbles does Jin have?

commonErrors.feedback: 10 ADDED 4 to Kim's 6 — that's '4 MORE than', a different comparison. '4 TIMES as many' multiplies: 4 × 6.
46 glued the digits 4 and 6 together. 'Times as many' means copies: four copies of 6 is 4 × 6 = 24.

steps.body: The comparison runs BACKWARD too. If Jin has 24 and that's '4 times as many as Kim,' then Kim's pile is the 24 **shared into 4 copies**: 24 ÷ 4 = 6. Times-as-many forward is multiplication; unwinding it is division — the same fact family you already own.

explanationVariants: Rosa's 20 is five copies of Ben's pile, so one copy is 20 ÷ 5 = 4 shells.

widget.prompt: Rosa has 20 shells — 5 TIMES as many as Ben. How many shells does Ben have?

commonErrors.feedback: 100 multiplied 20 × 5 — but Rosa's 20 already IS the five-copy pile. To find ONE copy (Ben's), divide: 20 ÷ 5.
15 subtracted 5 — that unwinds '5 MORE than'. '5 TIMES as many' unwinds by division: 20 ÷ 5 = 4.

widget.fallbackFeedback: Rosa's pile is 5 copies of Ben's — split it: 20 ÷ 5.

widget.prompt: Match each comparison to the bar picture that shows it.

left.label: "Ava has 3 times as many as Sam"

right.label: Ava's bar = Sam's bar repeated 3 times
Ava's bar = Sam's bar plus a little 3-piece

pairErrors.feedback: A little 3-piece tacked on shows '3 MORE'. '3 TIMES as many' repeats Sam's WHOLE bar three times — a much bigger stretch.

widget.missFeedback: TIMES copies the whole bar; MORE tacks on a fixed piece; SAME is equal bars.
widget.successFeedback: Times = whole-bar copies, more = a tacked-on piece, same = equal bars. The bar picture never lies.

explanationVariants: 12 is 2 more than 10 AND — checking copies — 12 isn't a whole-number multiple of 10, so 'times as many' language doesn't fit; Priya's 'more' claim is the accurate one.
Test the copy claim: 2 times as many as 10 would be 20, not 12. Only the '2 more' comparison matches 12.

widget.prompt: Sam has 10 cards; Dee has 12. Priya says 'Dee has 2 more.' Marco says 'Dee has 2 times as many.' Who's right?

options.label: Priya — 12 is 2 more than 10; 2 times as many would be 20
options.feedback: The copy test settles it: two copies of 10 is 20, not 12. Dee's edge is additive: +2.

options.label: Marco — 2 times as many
options.feedback: Two TIMES as many as 10 means two copies: 20. Dee has 12 — only 2 MORE, not 2 times.

options.label: Both say the same thing
options.feedback: They're very different claims: '2 more' adds 2 (→12); '2 times' copies the whole pile (→20). Only one matches Dee's 12.

options.label: Neither — you can't compare 10 and 12
options.feedback: You can, two ways: by gap (2 more) or by copies (1.2 times — not whole). The clean, true claim here is Priya's '2 more.'

hints: Two comparisons chain together — work one at a time.
Then Priya has 2 times Nia's pile.
explanationVariants: Chain the copies: Nia = 3 × 4 = 12, then Priya = 2 × 12 = 24 stickers.
Priya is 2 copies of (3 copies of 4) — 2 × 3 × 4 = 24.

widget.prompt: Owen has 4 stickers. Nia has 3 TIMES as many as Owen. Priya has 2 TIMES as many as Nia. How many stickers does Priya have?

commonErrors.feedback: 12 is NIA's pile (3 × 4) — Priya doubles that: 2 × 12 = 24.
9 added the comparison numbers to Owen's pile (4 + 3 + 2) — but each 'times' COPIES a whole pile: 3 × 4 = 12, then 2 × 12.

takeaways: 'n times as many' = n whole copies of the other pile — multiply.
Unwinding a times-as-many comparison is division (the fact family).
'Times' copies the whole bar; 'more' only tacks on a piece.
steps.teaser: next: turning comparison sentences into equations you can solve.

concept.body: Quick rewind. **'Times as many' is a copy machine.** '3 times as many as 5' feeds the whole 5-pile through three times: 5, 10, 15. Draw the other person's bar, then lay down that many copies of it.

explanationVariants: Bar picture: two 7-bars end to end reach 14.

widget.prompt: Ana has 7 pens. Ben has 2 TIMES as many. Ben has…

options.label: 9 pens
options.feedback: 9 added 2 — that's '2 MORE than'. Two TIMES copies the whole pile: 2 × 7 = 14.

options.label: 27 pens
options.feedback: 27 glued the digits together. Two copies of 7 is 2 × 7 = 14.
